name: Singapore Botanic Gardens
title: Ancient Trees in Singapore Botanic Gardens, Singapore: 8 to Find
meta_description: A UNESCO World Heritage garden's eight heritage trees, each with its own paperwork: a smuggled cannon ball seed, a moved baobab, a disputed banyan.
intro: Singapore's Botanic Gardens opened in 1859 and earned a UNESCO World Heritage listing in 2015, not for any single specimen but for grounds that have kept unusually good paperwork on the trees growing in them. A sausage tree arrived from Honolulu on 13 May 1931 and went into the ground that October, one of dozens of tropical trials from an era when a plant's usefulness decided its future. A cannon ball tree grew from a seed the assistant director E.J.H. Corner grabbed during a rushed eight-hour stop at the botanic garden in Peradeniya, Ceylon, the same year. A baobab, moved once in 1996 and only about forty years old, already carries five metres of girth, a fraction of the age a species that can pass a thousand years usually needs for that. A giant strangler fig by Swan Lake is registered as a Burmese banyan, though a 2024 study argues it is something else entirely, propagated here from cuttings for more than 150 years. A saga tree planted in the 1880s to smother weed grass now sits in the National Heritage Board's own art collection, photographed for a 2013 work mapping the island's saga trees. Two nutmeg trees near the old Economic Garden are what is left of the spice boom that gave Orchard Road its name. All eight stand on garden ground open daily and free to enter.
